Title:ChemE-as-Code: An Open-Source Platform for Agentic AI in Chemical Engineering
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:ChemE-as-Code provides an open-source environment in which AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) can carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it. Its calculation tools range from catalysis through process simulation to plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills tell a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git; calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package (simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets, relief) for USD 224 of API cost in the design sessions. Planted faults and engineering changes show that the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest, so they guide human review rather than replace it. No independent engineer has reviewed the design.

report.summary: ChemE-as-Code is an open-source platform that lets LLM agents perform traceable chemical-engineering calculations and checks, demoed on an ammonia design for $224 in API costs.
report.background: Chemical engineering design depends on simulation, P&IDs, HAZOP, life-cycle assessment, datasheets and relief calculations, all of which must be auditable and safety-checked. General-purpose LLMs can draft text and reason across tasks, but they are unreliable for numerical work and often hide how values were produced. That makes engineers reluctant to trust agent outputs in regulated, high-consequence settings. ChemE-as-Code responds by separating LLM reasoning from calculation engines, linking engineering files, and versioning artifacts in Git so results can be inspected. The preprint reflects a broader push toward domain-specific agentic AI: instead of a chatbot, the agent uses curated tools and skills inside an engineering workflow. It also tests whether open-source infrastructure can lower costs and vendor lock-in for early-stage design.
key_points: The platform provides an open-source environment where general-purpose LLM agents use curated skills and calculation tools spanning catalysis, process simulation, plant layout, HAZOP and life-cycle assessment. Engineers can inspect the same files and results.

Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git. Calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks flag inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line.

In an ammonia case, agents turned a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package including simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets and relief work for USD 224 of API cost across design sessions.

Planted faults and engineering changes showed the automated checks find only what their rules cover and miss the rest. The authors say checks guide human review rather than replace it, and no independent engineer reviewed the design.
report.impact: For the AI industry, ChemE-as-Code is a template for verifiable agentic work: keep the model away from raw calculation, attach provenance to every value, store artifacts in Git, and use CI-like checks. That is more credible than chat-only agents for regulated engineering. For developers, it shows how domain skills, external solvers and audit trails can be packaged into an open platform, though safety validation and rule coverage remain hard. For regular users and engineers, the promise is faster, cheaper early-stage design packages, but not autonomous certified engineering. The ammonia demo is illustrative and unreviewed, so the practical impact is a workflow prototype and benchmark, not a replacement for professional judgment.
report.tools: Watch the ChemE-as-Code paper and repository first. Related open-source tools include DWSIM for process simulation, Cantera for thermodynamics and kinetics, openLCA for life-cycle assessment, and Git/CI for versioned checks and provenance. Agent frameworks that can call external tools reliably are also relevant. HAZOP and P&ID work will likely still need commercial tools and human review.
